To invest with the office of prebendary; to present to a prebend. [Obs.] Grafton.
w.e: LL. praebendatus, p. p. of praebendari.

d: A prebendaryship. [Obs.] Foxe.
To calculate or determine beforehand; to prearrange. Masson.
One who prays. [R.] Coleridge.
w.e: L. precans, -antis, p. pr. of precari to pray.

d: 1. Depending on the will or pleasure of another; held by courtesy; liable to be changed or lost at the pleasure of another; as, precarious privileges. Addison.

2. Held by a doubtful tenure; depending on unknown causes or events; exposed to constant risk; not to be depended on for certainty or stability; uncertain; as, a precarious state of health; precarious fortunes. Intervals of partial and precarious liberty. Macaulay.
w.e: L. precarius obtained by begging or prayer, depending on request or on the will of another, fr. precari to pray, beg. See Pray.

d: The act of praying; supplication; entreaty. Cotton.

Preca*to*ry, a. “Suppliant; beseeching. Bp. Hopkins. Precatory words (Law), words of recommendation, request, entreaty, wish, or expectation, employed in wills, as distinguished from express directions; -- in some cases creating a trust. Jarman.”
w.e: L. precativus, precatorius, fr. precari to pray. See Precarious.

d: Preca*to*ry, a. “Suppliant; beseeching. Bp. Hopkins. Precatory words (Law), words of recommendation, request, entreaty, wish, or expectation, employed in wills, as distinguished from express directions; -- in some cases creating a trust. Jarman.”
w.e: L. precativus, precatorius, fr. precari to pray. See Precarious.

d: 1. Previous caution or care; caution previously employed to prevent mischief or secure good; as, his life was saved by precaution. They [ancient philosophers] treasured up their supposed discoveries with miserable precaution. J. H. Newman.
2. A measure taken beforehand to ward off evil or secure good or success; a precautionary act; as, to take precautions against accident.
w.e: F. précation, L. praecautio, fr. praecavere, praecautum, to guard against beforehand; prae before + cavere be on one's guard. See Pre-, and Caution.

d: 1. To warn or caution beforehand. Locke.
2. To take precaution against. [R.] Dryden.

n: a precautionary measure warding off impending danger or damage or injury etc.
he put an ice pack on the injury as a precaution
the trait of practicing caution in advance
judiciousness in avoiding harm or danger
he exercised caution in opening the door

d: Precautionary.

n: taken in advance to protect against possible danger or failure

d: Of or pertaining to precaution, or precautions; as, precautionary signals.

n: taken in advance to protect against possible danger or failure

d: Taking or using precaution; precautionary. -- Pre*cautious*ly, adv. -- Pre*cau*tious*ness, n.
Preceding; antecedent; previous. [Obs.] Hammond.
1. To go before in order of time; to occur first with relation to anything. Harm precedes not sin. Milton.
2. To go before in place, rank, or importance.
3. To cause to be preceded; to preface; to introduce; -- used with by or with before the instrumental object. [R.] It is usual to precede hostilities by a public declaration. Kent.
w.e: L. praecedere, praecessum; prae before + cedere to go, to be in motion: cf. F. préceder. See Pre-, and Cede.

n: furnish with a preface or introduction
She always precedes her lectures with a joke
move ahead (of others) in time or space
Bill preceded John in the long line of Susan's husbands
Most English adjectives precede the noun they modify

d: Pre*ceden*cy, n.
1. The act or state of preceding or going before in order of time; priority; as, one event has precedence of another.

2. The act or state of going or being before in rank or dignity, or the place of honor; right to a more honorable place; superior rank; as, barons have precedence of commoners. Which of them [the different desires] has the precedency in determining the will to the next action Locke.

n: status established in order of importance or urgency
...its precedence as the world's leading manufacturer of pharmaceuticals
the act of preceding in time or order or rank (as in a ceremony)

d: Pre*ceden*cy, n.
1. The act or state of preceding or going before in order of time; priority; as, one event has precedence of another.

2. The act or state of going or being before in rank or dignity, or the place of honor; right to a more honorable place; superior rank; as, barons have precedence of commoners. Which of them [the different desires] has the precedency in determining the will to the next action Locke.

n: status established in order of importance or urgency
...its precedence as the world's leading manufacturer of pharmaceuticals
the act of preceding in time or order or rank (as in a ceremony)

d: Going before; anterior; preceding; antecedent; as, precedent services. Shak. A precedent injury. Bacon. Condition precedent (Law), a condition which precede the vesting of an estate, or the accruing of a right.
w.e: L. praecedens, -entis, p. pr. of praecedere: cf. F. précédent. See Precede.

d: 1. Something done or said that may serve as an example to authorize a subsequent act of the same kind; an authoritative example. Examples for cases can but direct as precedents only. Hooker.
2. A preceding circumstance or condition; an antecedent; hence, a prognostic; a token; a sign. [Obs.]
3. A rough draught of a writing which precedes a finished copy. [Obs.] Shak.

4. (Law) “A judicial decision which serves as a rule for future determinations in similar or analogous cases; an authority to be followed in courts of justice; forms of proceeding to be followed in similar cases. Wharton.”

n: an example that is used to justify similar occurrences at a later time
a subject mentioned earlier (preceding in time)
preceding in time, order, or significance
(civil law) a law established by following earlier judicial decisions
a system of jurisprudence based on judicial precedents rather than statutory laws
common law originated in the unwritten laws of England and was later applied in the United States

d: Having a precedent; authorized or sanctioned by an example of a like kind. Walpole.

n: having or supported or justified by a precedent

d: Of the nature of a precedent; having force as an example for imitation; as, precedential transactions. All their actions in that time are not precedential to warrant posterity. Fuller.

n: having precedence (especially because of longer service)
precedential treatment for senior members of the firm

d: Beforehand; antecedently.
1. Going before; -- opposed to following.
2. (Astron.) “In the direction toward which stars appear to move. See Following, 2.”

n: of a person who has held and relinquished a position or office
a retiring member of the board

d: To surpass; to excel; to exceed. [Obs.] Howell.
Pre*cellen*cy, n. “Excellence; superiority. [Obs.] Sheldon.”
w.e: L. praecellentia, from praecellens, p. pr. of praecellere to excel, surpass: cf. OF. precellence.

d: Pre*cellen*cy, n. “Excellence; superiority. [Obs.] Sheldon.”
w.e: L. praecellentia, from praecellens, p. pr. of praecellere to excel, surpass: cf. OF. precellence.

d: Excellent; surpassing. [Obs.] Holland.

A leader of a choir; a directing singer. Specifically: (a) The leader of the choir in a cathedral; -- called also the chanter or master of the choir. Hook. (b) The leader of the congregational singing in Scottish and other churches.
w.e: L. praecentor, fr. praecinere to sing before; prae before + canere to sing. See Chant.

n: the musical director of a choir

d: The office of a precentor.

1. Any commandment, instruction, or order intended as an authoritative rule of action; esp., a command respecting moral conduct; an injunction; a rule. For precept must be upon precept. Isa. xxviii. 10. No arts are without their precepts. Dryden.
2. (Law) “A command in writing; a species of writ or process. Burrill.”
w.e: L. praeceptum, from praecipere to take beforehand, to instruct, teach; prae before + capere to take: cf. F. précepte. See Pre-, and Capacious.

d: To teach by precepts. [Obs.] Bacon.
Preceptive. [Obs.] [Passion] would give preceptial medicine to rage. Shak.
A precept. [R.] Bp. Hall.
Containing or giving precepts; of the nature of precepts; didactic; as, the preceptive parts of the Scriptures. The lesson given us here is preceptive to us. L'Estrange.
1. One who gives commands, or makes rules; specifically, the master or principal of a school; a teacher; an instructor.
2. The head of a preceptory among the Knights Templars. Sir W. Scott.
w.e: L. praeceptor, fr. praecipere to teach: cf. F. précepteur. See Precept.

n: teacher at a university or college (especially at Cambridge or Oxford)

d: Of or pertaining to a preceptor.
Preceptive. A law preceptory. Anderson (1573).

w.e: LL. praeceptoria an estate assigned to a preceptor, from L. praeceptor a commander, ruler, teacher, in LL., procurator, administrator among the Knights Templars. See Preceptor.

d: A woman who is the principal of a school; a female teacher.

The act of going before, or forward. Lunisolar precession. (Astron.) See under Lunisolar. -- Planetary precession, that part of the precession of the equinoxes which depends on the action of the planets alone. -- Precession of the equinoxes (Astron.), the slow backward motion of the equinoctial points along the ecliptic, at the rate of 50.2 annually, caused
w.e: L. praecedere, praecessum, to go before: cf. F. précession. See Precede.

n: the act of preceding in time or order or rank (as in a ceremony)
the motion of a spinning body (as a top) in which it wobbles so that the axis of rotation sweeps out a cone

d: Of or pertaining to pression; as, the precessional movement of the equinoxes.
A predecessor. [Obs.] Fuller.
An affected woman of polite society, esp. one of the literary women of the French salons of the 17th century.
1. The limit or exterior line encompassing a place; a boundary; a confine; limit of jurisdiction or authority; -- often in the plural; as, the precincts of a state. The precincts of light. Milton.
2. A district within certain boundaries; a minor territorial or jurisdictional division; as, an election precinct; a school precinct.
3. A parish or prescribed territory attached to a church, and taxed for its support. [U.S.] The parish, or precinct, shall proceed to a new choice. Laws of Massachusetts.
w.e: LL. praecinctum, fr. L. praecingere, praecinctum, to gird about, to encompass; prae before + cingere to gird, surround. See Pre-, and Cincture.

n: a district of a city or town marked out for administrative purposes

d: Preciousness; something precious. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

n: the quality of being fastidious or excessively refined

d: 1. Of great price; costly; as, a precious stone. The precious bane. Milton.

2. Of great value or worth; very valuable; highly esteemed; dear; beloved; as, precious recollections. She is more precious than rules. Prov. iii. 15. Many things which are most precious are neglected only because the value of them lieth hid. Hooker.

3. Particular; fastidious; overnice. [Obs.] Lest that precious folk be with me wroth. Chaucer. Precious metals, the uncommon and highly valuable metals, esp. gold and silver. -- Precious stones, gems; jewels.
w.e: OF. precious, precius, precios, F. précieux, L. pretiosus, fr. pretium price, worth, value. See Price.

n: diamonds, sapphires, rubies, and emeralds are precious stones
there is precious little time left
characterized by feeling or showing fond affection for
held in great esteem for admirable qualities especially of an intrinsic nature

d: In a precious manner; expensively; extremely; dearly. Also used ironically.

n: there is precious little time left

d: The quality or state of being precious; costliness; dearness.

n: the quality possessed by something with a great price or value
the positive quality of being precious and beyond value
the quality of being fastidious or excessively refined

d: 1. A sudden or headlong fall. [Obs.] Fuller.
2. A headlong steep; a very steep, perpendicular, or overhanging place; an abrupt declivity; a cliff. Where wealth like fruit on precipices grew. Dryden.
w.e: F. précipice, L. praecipitium, fr. praeceps, - cipitis, headlong; prae before + caput, capitis, the head. See Pre-, and Chief.

d: Commanding; directing.
w.e: L. praecipiens, p. pr. See Precept.

d: The quality or state of being precipitable.
Capable of being precipitated, or cast to the bottom, as a substance in solution. See Precipitate, n. (Chem.)

Pre*cipi*tan*cy, n. “The quality or state of being precipitant, or precipitate; headlong hurry; excessive or rash haste in resolving, forming an opinion, or executing a purpose; precipitation; as, the precipitancy of youth. Precipitance of judgment. I. Watts.”

n: the quality of happening with headlong haste or without warning

d: Pre*cipi*tan*cy, n. “The quality or state of being precipitant, or precipitate; headlong hurry; excessive or rash haste in resolving, forming an opinion, or executing a purpose; precipitation; as, the precipitancy of youth. Precipitance of judgment. I. Watts.”

n: the quality of happening with headlong haste or without warning

d: 1. Falling or rushing headlong; rushing swiftly, violently, or recklessly; moving precipitately. They leave their little lives Above the clouds, precipitant to earth. J. Philips. Should he return, that troop so blithe and bold, Precipitant in fear would wing their flight. Pope.
2. Unexpectedly or foolishly brought on or hastened; rashly hurried; hasty; sudden; reckless. Jer. Taylor. Precipitant rebellion. Eikon Basilike.
w.e: L. praecipitans, -antis, p. pr. of praecipitare: cf. F. précipitant. See Precipitate.

n: an agent that causes a precipitate to form
done with very great haste and without due deliberation
hasty marriage seldom proveth well"- Shakespeare

d: With rash or foolish haste; in headlong manner. Milton.
The quality or state of being precipitant; precipitation.
1. Overhasty; rash; as, the king was too precipitate in declaring war. Clarendon.
2. Lacking due deliberation or care; hurried; said or done before the time; as, a precipitate measure. The rapidity of our too precipitate course. Landor.
3. Falling, flowing, or rushing, with steep descent; headlong. Precipitate the furious torrent flows. Prior.
4. Ending quickly in death; brief and fatal; as, a precipitate case of disease. [Obs.] Arbuthnot.
w.e: L. praecipitatus, p. p. of praecipitare to precipitate, fr. praeceps headlong. See Precipice.

d: 1. To throw headlong; to cast down from a precipice or height. She and her horse had been precipitated to the pebbled region of the river. W. Irving.

2. To urge or press on with eager haste or violence; to cause to happen, or come to a crisis, suddenly or too soon; as, precipitate a journey, or a conflict. Back to his sight precipitates her steps. Glover. If they be daring, it may precipitate their designs, and prove dangerous. Bacon.

3. (Chem.) “To separate from a solution, or other medium, in the form of a precipitate; as, water precipitates camphor when in solution with alcohol. The light vapor of the preceding evening had been precipitated by the cold. W. Irving.”

n: a precipitated solid substance in suspension or after settling or filtering
separate as a fine suspension of solid particles
The bridge broke and precipitated the train into the river below
The crisis precipitated by Russia's revolution
Our economy precipitated into complete ruin
rain, snow and sleet were falling
done with very great haste and without due deliberation
hasty marriage seldom proveth well"- Shakespeare

d: In a precipitate manner; headlong; hastily; rashly. Swift.
1. The act of precipitating, or the state of being precipitated, or thrown headlong. In peril of precipitation From off rock Tarpeian. Shak.
2. A falling, flowing, or rushing downward with violence and rapidity. The hurry, precipitation, and rapid motion of the water, returning . . . towards the sea. Woodward.
3. Great hurry; rash, tumultuous haste; impetuosity. The precipitation of inexperience. Rambler.
4. (Chem.) “The act or process from a solution.”

n: he is responsible for the precipitation of his own demise
the act of casting down or falling headlong from a height
the falling to earth of any form of water (rain or snow or hail or sleet or mist)
the process of forming a chemical precipitate
the quantity of water falling to earth at a specific place within a specified period of time
the storm brought several inches of precipitation

d: One who precipitates, or urges on with vehemence or rashness. Hammond.

n: removes dust particles from gases by electrostatic precipitation

d: Precipitous. [Obs.] -- Preci*pitious*ly, adv. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.
1. Steep, like a precipice; as, a precipitous cliff or mountain.
2. Headlong; as, precipitous fall.
3. Hasty; rash; quick; sudden; precipitate; as, precipitous attempts. Sir T. Browne. Marian's low, precipitous Hush!' Mrs. Browning. -- Pre*cipi*tous*ly, adv. -- Pre*cipi*tous*ness, n.
w.e: L. praeceps, -cipitis: cf. OF. precipiteux. See Precipice.

n: done with very great haste and without due deliberation
hasty marriage seldom proveth well"- Shakespeare

d: A concise or abridged statement or view; an abstract; a summary.

n: a sketchy summary of the main points of an argument or theory

d: 1. Having determinate limitations; exactly or sharply defined or stated; definite; exact; nice; not vague or equivocal; as, precise rules of morality. The law in this point is not precise. Bacon. For the hour precise Exacts our parting hence. Milton.
2. Strictly adhering or conforming to rule; very nice or exact; punctilious in conduct or ceremony; formal; ceremonious. Addison. He was ever precise in promise-keeping. Shak.
w.e: L. praecisus cut off, brief, concise, p. p. of praecidere to cut off in front, to cut off; prae before + caedere to cut: cf. F. précis. Cf. Concise.

n: sharply exact or accurate or delimited
(of ideas, images, representations, expressions) characterized by perfect conformity to fact or truth

d: 1. One who limits, or restrains. [Obs.]

2. An overprecise person; one rigidly or ceremoniously exact in the observance of rules; a formalist; -- formerly applied to the English Puritans. The most dissolute cavaliers stood aghast at the dissoluteness of the emancipated precisian. Macaulay.
The quality or state of being a precisian; the practice of a precisian. Milton.
A precisian.
The quality or state of being precise; exact limitation; exactness; accuracy; strict conformity to a rule or a standard; definiteness. I have left out the utmost precisions of fractions. Locke.
w.e: Cf. F. précision, L. praecisio a cutting off. See Precise.

n: the quality of being reproducible in amount or performance
he handled it with the preciseness of an automaton

d: Cutting off; (Logic) exactly limiting by cutting off all that is not absolutely relative to the purpose; as, precisive censure; precisive abstraction. I. Watts.
1. To put a barrier before; hence, to shut out; to hinder; to stop; to impede. The valves preclude the blood from entering the veins. E. Darwin.

2. To shut out by anticipative action; to prevent or hinder by necessary consequence or implication; to deter action of, access to, employment of, etc.; to render ineffectual; to obviate by anticipation. This much will obviate and preclude the objections. Bentley.
w.e: L. praecludere, praeclusum; prae before + claudere to shut. See Close, v.

n: My sense of tact forbids an honest answer

d: The act of precluding, or the state of being precluded; a shutting out.

n: the act of preventing something by anticipating and disposing of it effectively

d: Shutting out; precluding, or tending to preclude; hindering. -- Pre*clusive*ly, adv.
Precocious. [Obs.]
1. Ripe or mature before the proper or natural time; early or prematurely ripe or developed; as, precocious trees. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

2. Developed more than is natural or usual at a given age; exceeding what is to be expected of one's years; too forward; -- used especially of mental forwardness; as, a precocious child; precocious talents.
w.e: L. praecox, -ocis, and praecoquus, fr. praecoquere to cook or ripen beforehand; prae before + coquere to cook. See 3d Cook, and cf. Apricot.

n: precocious flowers appear before the leaves as in some species of magnolias
characterized by or characteristic of exceptionally early development or maturity (especially in mental aptitude)

d: In a precocious manner.
Pre*coci*ty, n.

n: intelligence achieved far ahead of normal developmental schedules

d: Pre*coci*ty, n.

n: intelligence achieved far ahead of normal developmental schedules

d: One contemporary with, but older than, another. [Obs.] Fuller.
To cogitate beforehand. [R.] Sherwood.
w.e: L. praecogitatus, p. p. of praecogitare. See Pre-, and Cogitate.

d: Previous cogitation. [R.] Bailey.
1. Previous cognition. Fotherby.
2. (Scots Law) “A preliminary examination of a criminal case with reference to a prosecution. Erskine.”
w.e: L. praecognitio, fr. praecognoscere to foreknow. See Pre-, and Cognition.

n: knowledge of an event before it occurs

d: Cognizable beforehand.
A collection previously made. [R.]
To compose beforehand. Johnson.
An opinion or notion formed beforehand; a preconception. Hooker.
To conceive, or form an opinion of, beforehand; to form a previous notion or idea of. In a dead plain the way seemeth the longer, because the eye hath preconceived it shorter than the truth. Bacon.
The act of preconceiving; conception or opinion previously formed.

n: an opinion formed beforehand without adequate evidence
he did not even try to confirm his preconceptions
a partiality that prevents objective consideration of an issue or situation

d: To concert or arrange beforehand; to settle by previous agreement.
Something concerted or arranged beforehand; a previous agreement.
Previously arranged; agreed upon beforehand. -- Precon*certed*ly, adv. -- Precon*certed*ness, n.
The act of preconcerting; preconcert. Dr. T. Dwight.
To condemn beforehand. -- Pre*condem*nation, n.
A previous or antecedent condition; a preliminary condition.

n: a condition that is a prerequisite
put into the required condition beforehand
an assumption on which rests the validity or effect of something else
an assumption that is taken for granted

d: To conform by way anticipation. De Quincey.
Anticipative or antecedent conformity. Coleridge.
To proclaim; to publish; also, to summon; to call. [Obs.] Bp. Burnet.
1. A publishing by proclamation; a public proclamation. Bp. Hall.
2. (Eccl.) “A formal approbation by the pope of a person nominated to an ecclesiastical dignity. Addis & Arnold.”
w.e: L. praeconium a crying out in public, fr. praeco, -onis, a crier, a herald: cf. F. préconisation.

d: To conquer in anticipation. [R.] Fuller.
Of or pertaining to a state before consciousness.
A previous consent.
To consign beforehand; to make a previous consignment of.
Consolidated beforehand.
To constitute or establish beforehand.
To contract, engage, or stipulate previously.
To make a previous contract or agreement. Ayliffe.
A contract preceding another; especially (Law),
To contrive or plan beforehand.

w.e: Pref. pre- + L. cor, cordis, heart: cf. F. précordial.

d: A precursor. [Obs.] Shak.
A forerunning. [Obs.] Shak.
Preceding; introductory; precursory. A deep precursive sound. Coleridge.

One who, or that which, precedes an event, and indicates its approach; a forerunner; a harbinger. Evil thoughts are the invisible, airy precursors of all the storms and tempests of the soul. Buckminster.
w.e: L. praecursor, fr. praecurrere to run before; prae before + currere to run. See Course.

n: a person who goes before or announces the coming of another
a substance from which another substance is formed (especially by a metabolic reaction)
something that precedes and indicates the approach of something or someone

d: The position or condition of a precursor. Ruskin.
Preceding as a precursor or harbinger; indicating something to follow; as, precursory symptoms of a fever.
An introduction. [Obs.]
Living by prey; predatory. Derham.

n: living by or given to victimizing others for personal gain
hunting and killing other animals for food

d: Of or pertaining to prey; plundering; predatory. [R.] Boyse.
To date anticipation; to affix to (a document) an earlier than the actual date; to antedate; as, a predated deed or letter.

n: establish something as being earlier relative to something else

w.e: L. praedatio, fr. praedari to plunder.

n: the act of preying by a predator who kills and eats the prey
an act of plundering and pillaging and marauding

d: In a predatory manner.
1. Characterized by plundering; practicing rapine; plundering; pillaging; as, a predatory excursion; a predatory party. A predatory war. Macaulay.
2. Hungry; ravenous; as, predatory spirits. [Obs.] Exercise . . . maketh the spirits more hot and predatory. Bacon.
3. (Zoöl.) “Living by preying upon other animals; carnivorous.”
w.e: L. praedatorius, fr. praedari to plunder, fr. praeda prey. See Prey.

n: living by preying on other animals especially by catching living prey
characterized by plundering or pillaging or marauding
living by or given to victimizing others for personal gain

d: To prey; to plunder. [Obs.] Holinshed.
Prey; plunder; booty. [Obs.] Holinshed.
Premature decay.
To die sooner than. If children predecease progenitors. Shak.
The death of one person or thing before another. [R.] Brougham.
Going before; preceding. Our predecessive students. Massinger.

One who precedes; one who has preceded another in any state, position, office, etc.; one whom another follows or comes after, in any office or position. A prince who was as watchful as his predecessor had been over the interests of the state. Prescott.
w.e: L. praedecessor; prae before + decessor one who withdraws from the province he has governed, a retiring officer (with reference to his successor), a predecessor, fr. decedere: cf. F. prédécesseur. See

n: one who precedes you in time (as in holding a position or office)
something that precedes and indicates the approach of something or someone

d: To declare or announce beforehand; to preannounce. Milman.
A dedication made previously or beforehand.
To define beforehand.
Previous deliberation.
Previous delineation.

The step, or raised secondary part, of an altar; a superaltar; hence, in Italian painting, a band or frieze of several pictures running along the front of a superaltar, or forming a border or frame at the foot of an altarpiece.
To design or purpose beforehand; to predetermine. Mitford.
Of or pertaining to predestination; as, the predestinarian controversy. Waterland.
One who believes in or supports the doctrine of predestination. Dr. H. More.

n: anyone who submits to the belief that they are powerless to change their destiny

d: The system or doctrine of the predestinarians.

n: the belief or doctrine of predestinarians

d: Predestinarian. [Obs.] Heylin.
Predestinated; foreordained; fated. A predestinate scratched face. Shak.
w.e: L. praedestinatus, p. p. of praedestinare to predestine; prae before + destinare to determine. See Destine.

d: To predetermine or foreordain; to appoint or ordain beforehand by an unchangeable purpose or decree; to preëlect. Whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son. Rom. viii. 29.

n: foreordain by divine will or decree
his place in history was foreordained

d: 1. The act of predestinating. Predestination had overruled their will. Milton.
2. (Theol.) “The purpose of Good from eternity respecting all events; especially, the preordination of men to everlasting happiness or misery. See Calvinism.”

n: previous determination as if by destiny or fate

d: Determining beforehand; predestinating. [R.] Coleridge.
1. One who predestinates, or foreordains.

To decree beforehand; to foreordain; to predestinate. Young.

n: foreordain by divine will or decree

d: Predestination. [Obs.]
Capable of being determined beforehand. Coleridge.
Determined beforehand; as, the predeterminate counsel of God.
The act of previous determination; a purpose formed beforehand; as, the predetermination of God's will. Hammond.

n: the act of determining or ordaining in advance what is to take place
a mental determination or resolve in advance
he entered the argument with a predetermination to prove me wrong

d: 1. To determine (something) beforehand. Sir M. Hale.
2. To doom by previous decree; to foredoom.
w.e: Pref. pre- + determine: cf. F. prédéterminer.

d: To determine beforehand.
1. Consisting of land or farms; landed; as, predial estate; that is, real estate. Ayliffe.
2. Attached to land or farms; as, predial slaves.

Sagacious in adapting means to ends; circumspect in action, or in determining any line of conduct; practically wise; judicious; careful; discreet; sensible; -- opposed to rash; as, a prudent man; dictated or directed by prudence or wise forethought; evincing prudence; as, prudent behavior. Moses established a grave and prudent law. Milton.
2. Frugal; economical; not extravagant; as, a prudent woman; prudent expenditure of money.
w.e: L. prudens, -entis, contr. from providens: cf. F. prudent. See Provident.

d: 1. Proceeding from, or dictated or characterized by, prudence; prudent; discreet; sometimes, selfish or pecuniary as distinguished from higher motives or influences; as, prudential motives. A prudential line of conduct. Sir W. Scott.
2. Exercising prudence; discretionary; advisory; superintending or executive; as, a prudential committee.
